records.sourceFile: The influence of psychological factors on the incidence and severity of sports-related concussions - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Trinh LN, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. The Influence of Psychological Factors on the Incidence and Severity of Sports-Related Concussions: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: A systematic review, following PRISMA, of studies on whether preexisting emotional states, personality traits, temperament, life stressors and explanatory style affect the incidence and severity of sports-related concussion in athletes. Meanness, aggression and psychoticism were associated with more concussions, baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms with worse symptoms after concussion, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors with postconcussion syndrome in young athletes. The authors describe the evidence as low to moderate certainty.
paper.tldr: Some preexisting traits, such as meanness, aggression and psychoticism, were linked to more concussions in one study of football players, and baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness and depressive symptoms were linked to worse symptoms after concussion. Certainty is low to moderate, so these traits are not yet useful for screening individual athletes.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-guided search of PubMed, Embase, Medline and ScienceDirect, plus reference lists, covered English-language studies on preexisting psychological factors and concussion incidence or symptoms. Ten studies met inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively, because the designs were too heterogeneous for a meta-analysis. The review was registered with PROSPERO.
paper.findings: In 917 male football players, higher baseline negative emotionality, psychoticism, meanness, alienation and physically expressed aggression were associated with more concussions, and in 1,246 collegiate athletes higher agreeableness was associated with more unreported concussions (reported at P<.1). Higher baseline emotional or depressive symptoms were associated with worse post-concussion symptoms in two studies, and psychiatric illness, family history and life stressors were more common in young athletes (n=40) who developed postconcussion syndrome, although only 3 of the 40 had life stressors. Explanatory style was not associated with concussion incidence, but optimism was associated with longer recovery from complex concussions in one study.
paper.limitations: The patient groups and measures are heterogeneous, and some studies relied on self-reported concussion history, which may be inaccurate or underreported. Most participants were male, and many studies did not report incidence by sex. The conclusion lists pessimism among factors linked to higher incidence, but the explanatory style study found no incidence difference by optimism or pessimism, so the conclusion does not match the results.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes who report higher baseline irritability, sadness, nervousness or depressive symptoms may warrant closer monitoring after a concussion, as the authors suggest. A psychiatric history, family history or significant life stressors may flag young athletes at higher risk of postconcussion syndrome, but this rests on one small chart review. The authors suggest baseline psychological screening could help prevention and management, but the review does not test that.
paper.athleteDev: This review does not inform training or performance programming. Its only performance-linked finding is that extraversion and height predicted heading frequency in male soccer players, which does not set a training target.
paper.rtp: The review gives only general guidance for return to play: baseline emotional symptoms and psychiatric history may relate to post-concussion symptoms, and optimism was linked to longer recovery from complex concussions in one study. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance.

records.sourceFile: The relationship between mulitple concussions and multidimensional sleep quality in collegiate-aged, active athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Van Bortel KM, Hamill KE, Goeckner BD, Mayer AR, Brett BL, Meier TB. The relationship between multiple concussions and multidimensional sleep quality in collegiate-aged, active athletes. Sleep Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Objectives: to determine the association of cumulative concussion and repetitive head impacts with self-reported sleep quality in healthy collegiate-aged athletes. Methods: 212 athletes completed semistructured interviews on sport and concussion history and the PSQI. Concussions were counted under ACRM criteria, with CISG and LOC/PTA definitions as secondary metrics; repetitive head impact was measured by years of contact sport, age of first exposure and TES criteria. Results: more prior concussions were associated with higher PSQI global scores and poor sleep, with subscale effects on quality, latency, disturbances, medication use and daytime dysfunction; no repetitive head impact metric was associated with sleep. Conclusions: concussion history, not repetitive head impact exposure, is associated with worse self-reported sleep, mainly through subjective quality rather than duration.
paper.tldr: In 212 healthy collegiate-aged athletes, each additional prior concussion was linked to worse self-reported sleep, while contact-sport exposure was not. Sleep is worth asking about in athletes with a concussion history, but this cross-sectional study cannot show that concussion causes poor sleep.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 212 athletes aged 18 to 26 (62.7% male) in an active, healthy collegiate-aged cohort. Concussions were counted retrospectively from semistructured interviews under ACRM, CISG and LOC/PTA definitions, and repetitive head impact was estimated from years of contact sport, age of first exposure and TES criteria. Sleep was measured with the PSQI and analysed with general linear and logistic models adjusted for sex.
paper.findings: More prior concussions (ACRM) were associated with higher global PSQI scores (B = 0.50, p < .001) and poor sleep (OR = 1.52, p < .001). Concussions were associated with poorer sleep quality, longer latency, more disturbances, more sleep medication use and more daytime dysfunction, but not with sleep duration or efficiency. Years of contact sport, age of first exposure, TES criteria and contact vs noncontact sport were not associated with any sleep measure. Alternative concussion definitions gave similar results.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show direction, and reverse causation is possible. Concussion and exposure histories were recalled retrospectively, and sleep was self-reported with the PSQI rather than measured objectively. PSQI subscales were binarized on the response distribution, not clinical cut-offs, and secondary and exploratory analyses were not corrected for multiple comparisons. The authors note the sample was homogeneous and strictly screened.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete has a concussion history, ask about sleep latency, disturbances and daytime dysfunction, not only total hours slept. Do not use years of contact sport as a marker of sleep risk in this group, since it was not associated with sleep.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep quality questions can sit alongside concussion history in athlete profiles, since prior concussions tracked with worse subjective sleep in healthy collegiate athletes. Contact-sport years did not track with sleep, so they should not be used alone to flag sleep problems.
paper.rtp: This study can support asking about sleep when an athlete has a concussion history, but it cannot set return-to-sport timing. It excluded athletes concussed within the past 6 months or not fully recovered, so it does not describe sleep during recovery.

records.sourceFile: The role of personality traits in athlete selection - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Xu J, Hao F. The role of personality traits in athlete selection: A systematic review. Acta Psychologica. 2025;260:105478.
paper.abstract: The review asks which personality traits best predict athletic performance and through what mechanisms. Following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol, five databases were searched through March 2025, and 22 cross-sectional studies (N = 4,181 athletes) met the criteria. Higher conscientiousness and extraversion consistently predicted better performance, and neuroticism was negatively related. Three mechanisms are proposed: direct neurobiological effects, indirect psychological mediation, and contextual moderation by sport, level and culture. Conscientiousness, extraversion and low neuroticism are presented as robust predictors that could improve talent identification if assessed alongside sport and cultural context.
paper.tldr: Across 22 mostly cross-sectional studies of more than 4,000 participants, higher conscientiousness and extraversion and lower neuroticism went with better performance or selection status. The links are modest, mostly cross-sectional and vary by sport and level, so personality is best used as one input to talent identification rather than a selection rule.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251007053). Five databases (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science) were searched on 5 March 2025. Two reviewers screened 2,955 unique records, assessed 423 full texts and included 22 studies. Quality was rated with the STROBE checklist, and results were synthesised narratively because the heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Conscientiousness and extraversion were most often reported as positive predictors of performance, with effect sizes of about 0.26 to 0.70, and neuroticism was negatively related (up to -0.25). Some studies reported null associations, for example no significant link between Big Five traits and one-year post-draft performance in baseball. Trait-performance associations were reported as stronger in team sports than in individual sports in one study (interaction p < .05), and the authors describe sport and competitive level as moderators.
paper.limitations: Most included studies are cross-sectional (21 of 22, one quasi-longitudinal), several did not control for sex, sport, training history or culture, and personality instruments and performance measures varied widely. The summary effect range mixes different statistics (partial eta squared, Cohen's d, beta and r), and the baseball study is described both as null and as showing conscientiousness benefits, so individual results should be checked in the tables. The inclusion rule was athlete-only, yet several studies compare athletes with non-athlete groups, and the authors note that publication bias toward null results cannot be ruled out.
paper.practicalImplications: Use personality profiles as one input alongside physical testing, coach assessment and performance data in talent identification, rather than as a cut-off. Interpret the trait effects as modest and sport- and level-specific, since the review found they varied by context.
paper.athleteDev: Some included studies linked neuroticism or fear of negative evaluation to higher anxiety and lower performance under pressure, so trait profiles may help flag athletes for whom stress-management work is worth exploring. The review contains no intervention studies, so it does not show that changing traits or coaching them improves performance.
paper.rtp: The review addresses competitive athletes' selection and performance and does not study injury or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Thinking about elite performance - The experience and impact of mental fatigue in elite sport coaching.pdf

paper.citation: Russell S, Halson SL, Jenkins DG, Rynne SB, Roelands B, Kelly VG. Thinking About Elite Performance: The Experience and Impact of Mental Fatigue in Elite Sport Coaching. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Three elite netball coaches and performance staff rated mental fatigue, physical fatigue and readiness to perform each week through a 16-week preseason, and gave salivary samples for cortisol and alpha-amylase. Mental fatigue varied widely between individuals and was inversely related to readiness to perform.
paper.tldr: Elite coaching and performance staff can report high mental fatigue across a preseason, and higher fatigue tracks with lower readiness to coach. Workload and cognitively demanding tasks may need managing, although this small descriptive study cannot establish cause.
paper.methods: Case study of three staff at a professional Suncorp Super Netball team. Each week for 16 weeks, on the same morning, they completed 100 mm visual analogue scales for mental fatigue, physical fatigue and readiness to perform and gave a saliva sample. Repeated-measures correlations were used to relate the subjective measures.
paper.findings: Median mental fatigue ranged from 0 to 70.5 across the three coaches, with elevated ratings in weeks 8 and 12, after interstate double-header preseason matches, and in week 10, after a preseason tournament. Mental fatigue was inversely related to readiness to perform (r = -.44, P = .002) and positively related to physical fatigue (r = .67), while physical fatigue was not related to readiness (r = -.19, P = .208). The authors interpret the salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase values as indicating psychophysiological stress in all three staff members.
paper.limitations: Only three participants from a single team and season, with no control group. Ratings were weekly and salivary markers were not linked to any performance outcome. The confidence interval reported for the mental-physical fatigue correlation includes zero despite the significance claim, and the authors call for larger studies.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend educating staff about mental fatigue and strategies to manage or acutely reduce it. Elevated ratings followed travel for preseason matches and a preseason tournament, so those periods may be worth watching, although the study did not test any workload change.
paper.athleteDev: The study concerns coaches and staff rather than athletes, so it gives no direct evidence on athlete development. It suggests that staff fatigue during intensified periods may affect the quality of coach-athlete interactions, which the authors argue needs study.
paper.rtp: The study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot show whether staff mental fatigue affects injury management or return-to-play decisions.
